system.text:
You are a senior software engineer on a team that maintains a production Python codebase. You
have been handed one change request. You own it from understanding the requirement to delivering
code that a reviewer can approve and merge.

Your responsibilities

Understand the requirement.
- Read the request as the product team means it, not only its literal words. Work out the inputs,
  the expected outputs, the error cases and the edge cases it implies.
- Where the request is ambiguous, choose the interpretation most consistent with the rest of the
  system and with what users of the feature would expect.

Understand the code before changing it.
- Read the code you are changing and the code it depends on or that depends on it, as far as it is
  available to you. Know what a function does from its code, not only from its name.
- Know who calls what you change. Keep public interfaces, data formats and behaviour that other code
  relies on intact unless the request asks you to change them.

Make the change correctly.
- Correctness comes first: the new behaviour must be right for every input the request implies,
  including empty, missing, zero, negative, very large and malformed values where relevant.
- Handle errors the way the codebase does: fail clearly on invalid input; never silently return
  wrong data.
- Treat money, dates, units and identifiers with care: exact arithmetic where the codebase uses it,
  explicit units, no lossy conversions.
- Don't introduce security problems: validate untrusted input and keep secrets and personal data
  out of logs and output.

Keep the codebase healthy.
- Fit in with the surrounding code: its naming, structure, typing and error handling. A reviewer
  should not be able to tell which lines are new by their style.
- Keep the change as small as the request allows, and complete: every file the change needs, none
  it doesn't. Don't refactor, rename or reformat unrelated code.
- Write code that is simple and readable; add a docstring or comment where intent is not obvious.

Check your work.
- You cannot run the code, so verify it by reading it: trace the main path and each edge case
  through your change, check every import and name you use exists, and check that everything that
  calls the code you changed still works.
- Your change will be applied to the repository and checked by tests you do not see.

What you are given
- <task>: the change request from the product team.
- <context>: material from the repository. How much varies: it may be a single file or much of the
  project. It is what you know about the codebase.

What you can and cannot do
- You cannot run code, and there is no one to ask.
- If tools are provided with this request, you may use them to look at the repository before you
  answer. If no tools are provided, you cannot open files or search: deliver the finished change in
  this reply. Tool calls, plans and requests for more files written as text are not executed, and a
  reply without code counts as no change.
- If something you need is not shown, make the most reasonable assumption consistent with what is
  shown, and implement it.

Output format (strict)
Your reply is the code change itself. Return the complete new contents of every file you create or
modify, each wrapped exactly as:
<file path="PATH">
...full file contents...
</file>
- Replace PATH with the file's real path relative to the repository root, as shown in <context> or
  <task>.
- Always the whole file, never a diff or an excerpt, and no placeholders such as "rest unchanged".
- Files you don't change are left out.
- Return nothing outside the <file> blocks: no explanations, plans or summaries before or after them.

user.text:
Support agents want the order references in a customer's message turned into links. Add
`order_refs(text)` in a new module `shopkit/support/linking.py`. It returns the order references
mentioned in the text, in the order they first appear and without duplicates, each written the way
the shop writes that kind of reference everywhere else. Customers type them in all sorts of ways:
"so 2019 123", "SO-2019-000123", "ORD_1A2B3C4D5E6F". Anything that isn't a valid order reference is
left out.

"""Identifiers. Internal ids are prefixed random hex; customer-facing codes avoid look-alike characters."""
import secrets

# No 0/O, 1/I/L: these codes get read out over the phone and typed from printed slips.
_CODE_ALPHABET = "ABCDEFGHJKMNPQRSTUVWXYZ23456789"


def new_id(prefix: str) -> str:
    """e.g. new_id("ord") -> "ord_3f9a1c2b7d4e"."""
    return f"{prefix}_{secrets.token_hex(6)}"


def short_code(length: int = 8, groups: int = 0) -> str:
    """Random human-friendly code from an unambiguous alphabet, e.g. "K7QM-X2PA" with groups=4.
    groups=0 means no dashes."""
    code = "".join(secrets.choice(_CODE_ALPHABET) for _ in range(length))
    if groups:
        code = "-".join(code[i:i + groups] for i in range(0, len(code), groups))
    return code


def is_short_code(text: str) -> bool:
    return bool(text) and all(c in _CODE_ALPHABET or c == "-" for c in text)

"""Find order references in free text so they can be turned into links.

Support agents want the order references in a customer's message highlighted,
but customers type them in all sorts of ways: "so 2019 123", "SO-2019-000123",
"ORD_1A2B3C4D5E6F".  We pick out the runs that could be a storefront id
(ord_<12 hex>) or a sales order reference (SO/SOB-year-sequence), keep only
what the shop's own reference parser accepts, and return each one in the form
the shop prints it.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import re

from shopkit.core.order_engine import formatOrderRef, parseOrderRef

# Candidate runs in free text, matched as wide as plausible so an invalid tail
# attaches to the reference and gets rejected instead of leaving a
# valid-looking prefix behind: a storefront id (ord_ then up to 13 hex chars)
# or SO/SOB with a year and a sequence, spaces or dashes (or both) between the
# parts.  The trailing lookahead keeps "SO-2019-12-3" and "SO-2019-12345678"
# unmatched.  Actual validity (year >= 2017, sequence at most 6 digits, exact
# hex id) is parseOrderRef's job.
_REF_CANDIDATE = re.compile(
    r"\b(ord_[0-9a-f]{0,13}|so[b]?[\s-]*\d{1,5}[\s-]*\d{0,7})(?![\d-])",
    re.I,
)


def order_refs(text: str) -> list[str]:
    """Order references mentioned in *text*, in the order they first appear.

    Each reference is returned the way the shop writes that kind of reference
    ("SO-2019-000123", "ord_1a2b3c4d5e6f") regardless of how it was typed
    ("so 2019 123", "SO-2019-000123", "ORD_1A2B3C4D5E6F", ...).  Runs that
    are not valid order references are left out, and a reference that is
    mentioned more than once is only returned once."""
    if text is None:
        return []
    refs: list[str] = []
    seen: set[str] = set()
    for candidate in _REF_CANDIDATE.finditer(text):
        parsed = parseOrderRef(candidate.group(0))
        if parsed is None:
            continue
        ref = formatOrderRef(*parsed)
        if ref not in seen:
            seen.add(ref)
            refs.append(ref)
    return refs

```python
"""Find order references in free text so they can be turned into links.

Support agents want the order references in a customer's message highlighted,
but customers type them in all sorts of ways: "so 2019 123", "SO-2019-000123",
"ORD_1A2B3C4D5E6F".  We pick out the runs that could be a storefront id
(ord_<12 hex>) or a sales order reference (SO/SOB-year-sequence), keep only
what the shop's own reference parser accepts, and return each one in the form
the shop prints it.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import re

from shopkit.core.order_engine import formatOrderRef, parseOrderRef

# Candidate runs in free text, widest first so invalid tails attach to the
# reference and get rejected rather than leaving a valid-looking prefix:
# a storefront id (ord_ then up to 13 hex chars) or SO/SOB, a 4-digit-ish year
# and a sequence with spaces or dashes between the parts.  The trailing
# lookahead keeps "SO-2019-12-3" / "SO-2019-12345678" unmatched.  Validity
# (year >= 2017, sequence length, exact hex id) is parseOrderRef's job.
_REF_CANDIDATE = re.compile(
    r"\b(ord_[0-9a-f]{0,13}|so[b]?[\s-]*\d{1,5}[\s-]*\d{0,7})(?![\d-])",
    re.I,
)


def order_refs(text: str) -> list[str]:
    """Order references mentioned in *text*, in the order they first appear.

    Each reference is returned the way the shop writes that kind of reference
    ("SO-2019-000123", "ord_1a2b3c4d5e6f") regardless of how it was typed
    ("so 2019 123", "SO-2019-000123", "ORD_1A2B3C4D5E6F", ...).  Runs that
    are not valid order references are left out, and a reference that is
    mentioned more than once is only returned once."""
    if text is None:
        return []
    refs: list[str] = []
    seen: set[str] = set()
    for candidate in _REF_CANDIDATE.finditer(text):
        parsed = parseOrderRef(candidate.group(0))
        if parsed is None:
            continue
        ref = formatOrderRef(*parsed)
        if ref not in seen:
            seen.add(ref)
            refs.append(ref)
    return refs
```

```python
def order_refs(text: str) -> list[str]:
    """Order references mentioned in *text*, first-appearance order, deduped.

    Each reference is returned in the form the shop writes it in (see
    formatOrderRef): "SO-2019-000123", "SOB-2020-000045", "ord_1a2b3c4d5e6f".
    Customers type refs with dashes, spaces or neither and in any case; a
    candidate is only kept if parseOrderRef accepts it, so years before 2017,
    too-long sequences and malformed ids are left out."""
    seen: dict[str, None] = {}
    for m in _REF_SCAN.finditer(text or ""):
        parsed = parseOrderRef(m.group(1))
        if parsed is None:
            continue
        ref = formatOrderRef(*parsed)
        seen.setdefault(ref, None)
    return list(seen)
```

```python
"""Turn the order references a customer types into the canonical references the shop uses.

Support agents paste customer messages that contain order references in all sorts of
typographic forms ("so 2019 123", "SO-2019-000123", "ORD_1A2B3C4D5E6F"). This module finds
them and rewrites each one the way the shop writes that kind of reference everywhere else
(see shopkit.core.order_engine.formatOrderRef), so the agent can link them.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import re

from shopkit.core.order_engine import formatOrderRef, parseOrderRef

# A reference embedded in free text. Two shapes, matching what parseOrderRef accepts:
#   - sales order: "SO-2019-000123", "SOB 2020 45", "so 2019 123" (spaces act as dashes,
#     case-insensitive; the sequence is 1-6 digits)
#   - storefront id: "ord_1a2b3c4d5e6f" (12 hex, case-insensitive)
# The trailing \b keeps a run of more digits/hex from matching as a shorter valid ref.
_REF = re.compile(
    r"\bSOB?[ -]*\d{4}[ -]*\d{1,6}\b"
    r"|\bord_[0-9a-f]{12}\b",
    re.IGNORECASE,
)


def order_refs(text):
    """Return the order references in *text*, in the order they first appear, without
    duplicates, each written the way the shop writes that kind of reference.

    Only references that parseOrderRef accepts are kept; anything else is left out."""
    found = []
    seen = set()
    for m in _REF.finditer(text or ""):
        parsed = parseOrderRef(m.group(0))
        if parsed is None:
            continue
        kind, year, seq = parsed
        ref = formatOrderRef(kind, year, seq)
        if ref not in seen:
            seen.add(ref)
            found.append(ref)
    return found
```

```python
"""Turn the order references a customer writes into the canonical references the shop uses.

Customers paste order references in all sorts of forms ("so 2019 123", "SO-2019-000123",
"ORD_1A2B3C4D5E6F"). order_refs finds them in a message and rewrites each the way the shop
writes that kind of reference everywhere else (shopkit.core.order_engine.formatOrderRef), so
support agents can link them.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import re

from shopkit.core.order_engine import formatOrderRef, parseOrderRef

# An order reference embedded in free text, in the two shapes parseOrderRef accepts:
#   * sales order: "SO-2019-000123", "SOB 2020 45", "so 2019 123" -- prefix is SO/SOB, a 4-digit
#     year, and a 1-6 digit sequence; spaces act like dashes and case is ignored
#   * storefront id: "ord_1a2b3c4d5e6f" -- ord_ followed by exactly 12 hex digits
# The trailing \b keeps a longer run of digits/hex from matching as a shorter, valid-looking ref.
_REF = re.compile(
    r"\bSOB?[- ]*\d{4}[- ]*\d{1,6}\b|\bord_[0-9a-f]{12}\b",
    re.IGNORECASE,
)


def order_refs(text: str) -> list[str]:
    """Return the order references in *text*, in the order they first appear and without
    duplicates, each written the way the shop writes that kind of reference.

    Anything that parseOrderRef does not accept is left out."""
    refs: list[str] = []
    seen: set[str] = set()
    for match in _REF.finditer(text or ""):
        parsed = parseOrderRef(match.group(0))
        if parsed is None:
            continue
        kind, year, seq = parsed
        ref = formatOrderRef(kind, year, seq)
        if ref not in seen:
            seen.add(ref)
            refs.append(ref)
    return refs
```

```python
    r"\b(ord_[0-9a-f]+|sob?[ -]*\d{4}[ -]*\d{1,6}(?:-\d+)*)\b",
    re.IGNORECASE,
)


def order_refs(text: str) -> list[str]:
    """Order references mentioned in text, in first-occurrence order, without duplicates.

    Each is normalized to the shop's canonical form: "SO-2019-000123" (or "SOB-...")
    and "ord_1a2b3c4d5e6f", via formatOrderRef. Anything parseOrderRef rejects -- a
    pre-2017 year, a too-long sequence, a mangled id -- is left out."""
    refs: list[str] = []
    seen: set[str] = set()
    for m in _REF_CANDIDATE.finditer(text or ""):
        parsed = parseOrderRef(m.group(1))
        if parsed is None:
            continue
        ref = formatOrderRef(*parsed)
        if ref not in seen:
            seen.add(ref)
            refs.append(ref)
    return refs
```

```python
        if parsed is None:

        ref = formatOrderRef(*parsed)
        if ref not in seen:
            seen.add(ref)
            refs.append(ref)
    return refs
```

```python
"""Find order references in free text so they can be turned into links.

Support agents want the order references in a customer's message highlighted,
but customers type them in all sorts of ways: "so 2019 123", "SO-2019-000123",
"ORD_1A2B3C4D5E6F".  We pick out the runs that could be a storefront id
(ord_<12 hex>) or a sales order reference (SO/SOB-year-sequence), keep only
what the shop's own reference parser accepts, and return each one in the form
the shop prints it.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import re

from shopkit.core.order_engine import formatOrderRef, parseOrderRef

# Candidate runs in free text, widest first so invalid tails attach to the
# reference and get rejected rather than leaving a valid-looking prefix:
# a storefront id (ord_ then up to 13 hex chars) or SO/SOB, a 4-digit-ish year
# and a sequence with spaces or dashes between the parts.  The trailing
# lookahead keeps "SO-2019-12-3" / "SO-2019-12345678" unmatched.  Validity
# (year >= 2017, sequence length, exact hex id) is parseOrderRef's job.
_REF_CANDIDATE = re.compile(
    r"\b(ord_[0-9a-f]{0,13}|so[b]?[\s-]*\d{1,5}[\s-]*\d{0,7})(?![\d-])",
    re.I,
)


def order_refs(text: str) -> list[str]:
    """Order references mentioned in *text*, in the order they first appear.

    Each reference is returned the way the shop writes that kind of reference
    ("SO-2019-000123", "ord_1a2b3c4d5e6f") regardless of how it was typed
    ("so 2019 123", "SO-2019-000123", "ORD_1A2B3C4D5E6F", ...).  Runs that
    are not valid order references are left out, and a reference that is
    mentioned more than once is only returned once."""
    if text is None:
        return []
    refs: list[str] = []
    seen: set[str] = set()
    for candidate in _REF_CANDIDATE.finditer(text):
        parsed = parseOrderRef(candidate.group(0))
        if parsed is None:
            continue
        ref = formatOrderRef(*parsed)
        if ref not in seen:
            seen.add(ref)
            refs.append(ref)
    return refs
```

"""Find order references in free text so they can be turned into links.

Support agents want the order references in a customer's message highlighted,
but customers type them in all sorts of ways: "so 2019 123", "SO-2019-000123",
"ORD_1A2B3C4D5E6F".  We pick out the runs that could be a storefront id
(ord_<12 hex>) or a sales order reference (SO/SOB-year-sequence), keep only
what the shop's own reference parser accepts, and return each one in the form
the shop prints it.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import re

from shopkit.core.order_engine import formatOrderRef, parseOrderRef

# Candidate runs in free text, matched as wide as plausible so an invalid tail
# attaches to the reference and gets rejected instead of leaving a
# valid-looking prefix behind: a storefront id (ord_ then up to 13 hex chars)
# or SO/SOB with a year and a sequence, spaces or dashes (or both) between the
# parts.  The trailing lookahead keeps "SO-2019-12-3" and "SO-2019-12345678"
# unmatched.  Actual validity (year >= 2017, sequence at most 6 digits, exact
# hex id) is parseOrderRef's job.
_REF_CANDIDATE = re.compile(
    r"\b(ord_[0-9a-f]{0,13}|so[b]?[\s-]*\d{1,5}[\s-]*\d{0,7})(?![\d-])",
    re.I,
)


def order_refs(text: str) -> list[str]:
    """Order references mentioned in *text*, in the order they first appear.

    Each reference is returned the way the shop writes that kind of reference
    ("SO-2019-000123", "ord_1a2b3c4d5e6f") regardless of how it was typed
    ("so 2019 123", "SO-2019-000123", "ORD_1A2B3C4D5E6F", ...).  Runs that
    are not valid order references are left out, and a reference that is
    mentioned more than once is only returned once."""
    if text is None:
        return []
    refs: list[str] = []
    seen: set[str] = set()
    for candidate in _REF_CANDIDATE.finditer(text):
        parsed = parseOrderRef(candidate.group(0))
        if parsed is None:
            continue
        ref = formatOrderRef(*parsed)
        if ref not in seen:
            seen.add(ref)
            refs.append(ref)
    return refs
